rv.q: This superlative staging leaves behind soul ache accompanied by the exhilaration of a fresh encounter with a great work of theater revitalized anew.
This production plays the laughs excellently but also proves that love – twisted and damaged, perhaps – is at the heart of this play.
This is a visceral, devastating, deeply human night.

It’s impossible to imagine the shock visited upon Broadway by Edward Albee’s Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? when it opened 50 years ago: the ancient taboos casually obliterated with tossed-off one-liners; the antic sexual frankness; the naked rage; the deepening, satanic night of drinking and verbal dagger-play, continuing relentlessly until ev...

And the good news is that they haven’t aged a bit. Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf, Edward Albee’s seminal and searing portrait of a viciously feuding, functionally alcoholic, codependently miserable and mildly delusional married couple, opened Saturday night at the Booth Theatre, 50 years to the day after its Broadway debut.
Veterans of past productions may feel that Albee's drama has yielded all that it has to offer. But this unmissable revival shows otherwise.
Each put-down, no matter how oblique, exposes a raw nerve.

Steered to that level of hard, vivid reality by MacKinnon’s keen eye and pitch-perfect ear for group rhythms, this may be the finest Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? for years to come: brutally honest, bitingly funny, and confidently owned by four gutsy, cunning, powerhouse actors.
The production is powerful, revealing and as painful as a fresh wound.

As the guests, Nick and Honey, Madison Dirks and Carrie Coon are fine foils. Dirks' slick Nick, who quickly becomes the target of George's bitterness and Martha's lust, captures the hollowness and impotence (on several levels) that define his role. Coon's Honey is at once fetching and pitiable, and a marvelously fluid drunk.
It’s perhaps less surprising that the revival of "Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?" is devilishly engrossing — Edward Albee’s 1962 masterwork is a superb play — than how it works its sorcery.
Indeed, it is as literal and close to the bone Albee as one could hope to find.
Each of those expertly drawn characters, forcefully directed by Pam MacKinnon, commits sizzling, psychological mayhem on the other.

tn.cat: Best Featured Actress in a Play

cn.t: This 50th anniversary revival of Albee's masterpiece earns near-universal acclaim for its shattering emotional intensity and brilliant Steppenwolf leads, proving the marital warfare drama remains as devastating and immediate as ever.

sg.ra: The Booth is one of Broadway's smallest houses at 766 seats, so center orchestra rows C-H give close-up detail of plays and intimate dramas without paying the very-front premium. Row AA front offers max legroom (Headout) but stage is high; step back a few rows for better sightline onto the stage floor.

sg.vl: Workable angle, not the sweet spot
sg.ra: Booth is narrow so side orchestra remains viable, but a 2018 BWW forum post specifically flagged 'angle from the front side seats' as a concern. Closer rows (BB, A) on the side get awkward angles onto the high stage. Mid-house aisle seats recover the view while adding legroom.
sg.rr: A-P (17 rows, odd 1-15 left, even 2-16 right)

sg.ra: In a 252-seat mezzanine with only 8 rows, even the back row is close. SeatPlan and Headout both call Center Mezz A-B some of the best seats in the house, and G-H are cited as strong value. With the Booth's intimate scale, the mezzanine never feels distant — this is the value pick.

sg.vl: Small house saves the side angle
sg.ra: SeatPlan explicitly notes side-mezz views are 'slightly more angled but still viable' because the Booth is narrow. Decent budget alternative, but the center mezz is a better value at similar price tier so this is solid-not-sweet.
